claim: The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (India) conducted a serosurvey across its constituent laboratories and centers across India in August and September 2020.
source: To understand the spread of SARS-CoV2, in August and September 2020, the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (India) conducted a serosurvey across its constituent laboratories and centers across India.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the study design and timing.

claim: Of 10,427 volunteers, 1058 (10.14%) tested positive for SARS-CoV2 anti-nucleocapsid (anti-NC) antibodies.
source: Of 10,427 volunteers, 1058 (10.14%) tested positive for SARS-CoV2 anti-nucleocapsid (anti-NC) antibodies
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study's serological testing results.

claim: 95% of seropositive subjects had surrogate neutralization activity.
source: 95% of which had surrogate neutralization activity
evidence: This is a measured outcome from the neutralization antibody testing performed on seropositive samples.

claim: Three-fourths of seropositive subjects recalled no symptoms.
source: Three-fourth of these recalled no symptoms.
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data collected from seropositive participants.

claim: Repeat serology tests at 3 months (n = 607) showed stable anti-NC antibodies.
source: Repeat serology tests at 3 (n = 607) and 6 (n = 175) months showed stable anti-NC antibodies
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements of antibody levels.

claim: Repeat serology tests at 3 months showed declining neutralization activity.
source: Repeat serology tests at 3 (n = 607) and 6 (n = 175) months showed stable anti-NC antibodies but declining neutralization activity.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements of neutralization activity.

claim: Local seropositivity was higher in densely populated cities.
source: Local seropositivity was higher in densely populated cities
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between population density and seropositivity rates across different locations.

claim: Local seropositivity was inversely correlated with a 30-day change in regional test positivity rates (TPRs).
source: Local seropositivity was higher in densely populated cities and was inversely correlated with a 30-day change in regional test positivity rates (TPRs).
evidence: This is based on statistical correlation analysis between seropositivity and changes in TPR.

claim: Regional seropositivity above 10% was associated with declining TPR.
source: Regional seropositivity above 10% was associated with declining TPR.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between seropositivity thresholds and TPR trends.

claim: High-exposure work was associated with higher odds of seropositivity (odds ratio 2.23, 95% confidence interval 1.92–2.59, p<0.0001).
source: Personal factors associated with higher odds of seropositivity were high-exposure work (odds ratio, 95% confidence interval, p value: 2.23, 1.92–2.59, <0.0001)
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Use of public transport was associated with higher odds of seropositivity (odds ratio 1.79, 95% confidence interval 1.43–2.24, p<0.0001).
source: use of public transport (1.79, 1.43–2.24, <0.0001)
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Not smoking was associated with higher odds of seropositivity (odds ratio 1.52, 95% confidence interval 1.16–1.99, p=0.0257).
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: Non-vegetarian diet was associated with higher odds of seropositivity (odds ratio 1.67, 95% confidence interval 1.41–1.99, p<0.0001).
source: non-vegetarian diet (1.67, 1.41–1.99, <0.0001)
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of questionnaire data.

claim: B blood group was associated with higher odds of seropositivity (odds ratio 1.36, 95% confidence interval 1.15–1.61, p=0.001).
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of blood group data.

claim: The World Health Organization declared SARS-CoV-2 infection as a pandemic on March 11, 2020.
source: The World Health Organization declared SARS-CoV-2 infection as a pandemic on March 11, 2020 (WHO, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2020.

claim: India announced a lockdown strategy within 2 weeks of the WHO pandemic declaration.
source: Within 2 weeks, India announced a lockdown strategy that severely influenced the growth of the pandemic
evidence: This is a statement about the timing of India's policy response.

claim: Early literature pointed towards asymptomatic transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Early literature pointed towards asymptomatic transmission of SARS-CoV-2 and raised the need for extended testing (Nishiura et al., 2020; Bai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nishiura et al., 2020 and Bai et al., 2020.

claim: Serosurveillance revealed that many more were probably getting infected without manifesting symptoms.
source: While RT-PCR was an undisputed choice for establishing a positive infection, serosurveillance revealed that many more were probably getting infected without manifesting symptoms (Brown and Walensky, 2020; Oran and Topol, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brown and Walensky, 2020 and Oran and Topol, 2020.

claim: Initial estimates of asymptomatic infection rate from the West were around 40–45%.
source: Initial estimates of asymptomatic infection rate from the West were around 40–45% (Oran and Topol, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oran and Topol, 2020.

claim: The first case of Covid in India was reported on January 30, 2020.
source: In India, the first case of Covid was reported on January 30, 2020 (Andrews et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andrews et al., 2020.

claim: Serological surveys confirmed that spread beyond the Indian megacities was minimal in early May–June, with less than 1% seropositivity outside the designated containment zones.
source: Serological surveys have confirmed that spread beyond the Indian megacities was minimal in early May–June, with less than 1% seropositivity outside the designated containment zones, suggesting that the lockdown had been effective in limiting the spread (Murhekar et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Murhekar et al., 2020a.

claim: The lockdown had been effective in limiting the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in India.
source: Serological surveys have confirmed that spread beyond the Indian megacities was minimal in early May–June, with less than 1% seropositivity outside the designated containment zones, suggesting that the lockdown had been effective in limiting the spread (Murhekar et al., 2020a).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low seropositivity data, supported by citation to Murhekar et al., 2020a.

claim: By the end of June, migrant workforces caught in the cities during the lockdown were sent to their rural homes.
source: By the end of June, migrant workforces caught in the cities during the lockdown were sent to their rural homes, which may have led to subsequent rapid, multifocal rise in cases in July 2020.
evidence: This is a statement about a known policy and demographic event in India.

claim: The migration of workers may have led to subsequent rapid, multifocal rise in cases in July 2020.
source: By the end of June, migrant workforces caught in the cities during the lockdown were sent to their rural homes, which may have led to subsequent rapid, multifocal rise in cases in July 2020.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the causal relationship between migration and case increases.

claim: By October 2020, total new cases began to decline with further outbreaks limited to a few geographies.
source: By October 2020, total new cases began to decline with further outbreaks limited to a few geographies.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiological trajectory based on known data.

claim: A national serosurvey in 70 districts of India conducted by ICMR had a reported crude positivity rate of about 10%.
source: A national serosurvey in 70 districts of India, conducted by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), had a reported crude positivity rate of about 10% (Murhekar et al., 2020b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Murhekar et al., 2020b.

claim: The ICMR survey is not representative of Indian cities.
source: Since only a few districts of India account for the majority of urban areas, the ICMR survey is not representative of Indian cities (Murhekar et al., 2020a)
evidence: This is an inference about the representativeness of the ICMR survey, with reference to Murhekar et al., 2020a.

claim: A combination of higher population density and indoor lives has led to greater spread of disease in urban areas than rural areas.
source: where a combination of higher population density and indoor lives has led to greater spread of disease than rural areas
evidence: This is an inference based on known epidemiological patterns.

claim: Existing city-wise serosurveys are variable in target population as well as methodology and cannot be easily compared.
source: Existing city-wise serosurveys are variable in target population as well as methodology and cannot be easily compared to determine the relative course of the pandemic (Ray et al., 2020; Satpati et al., 2020; Babu et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Ray et al., 2020; Satpati et al., 2020; Babu et al., 2020; Sharma et al., 2020).

claim: The CSIR cohort includes permanent staff, families of staff members, students, and temporary employees providing support services.
source: Though limited by not being a population-denominated study, the cohort includes permanent staff, families of staff members, students, and temporary employees proving support services such as security, sanitation, housekeeping, etc.
evidence: This is a description of the study population.

claim: The CSIR cohort is a diverse microcosm of India encompassing multiple socioeconomic groups.
source: This is a diverse microcosm of India encompassing multiple socioeconomic groups
evidence: This is a characterization of the study population.

claim: The average seropositivity was 10.14% (95% confidence interval 9.6–10.7).
source: In 10,427 subjects from over 17 states and 2 union territories, the average seropositivity was 10.14% (95% confidence interval [CI] 9.6–10.7)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the study's serological testing results.

claim: Seropositivity varied widely across locations.
source: In 10,427 subjects from over 17 states and 2 union territories, the average seropositivity was 10.14% (95% confidence interval [CI] 9.6–10.7), but varied widely across locations (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on the data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Seropositivity was greater in regions with higher population density.
source: As expected from the known outward spread of infection from large Indian cities, seropositivity was greater in regions with higher population density (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Lab-wise seropositivity was correlated with the regional change in TPR.
source: Lab-wise seropositivity was correlated with the regional change in TPR.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of seropositivity and TPR changes.

claim: Regional transmission of SARS-CoV2 was inversely correlated to local seropositivity.
source: By this measure, regional transmission of SARS-CoV2 was inversely correlated to local seropositivity (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Seropositivity of 10% or more was associated with reductions in TPR.
source: Seropositivity of 10% or more was associated with reductions in TPR, which may mean declining transmission (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on the data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Out of 861 seropositive subjects who provided data on symptomatology, 647 subjects (75.3%) did not recall any of the nine symptoms asked for.
source: Out of 861 seropositive subjects who also provided data on symptomatology, 647 subjects (75.3%) did not recall any of the nine symptoms asked for (two of these did not provide gender data) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data from seropositive participants.

claim: Among symptomatic subjects, fever (~50%) was the most frequent symptom.
source: Among the minority of subjects with symptoms, the most reported symptom constellation was those of a mild flu-like disease with fever (~50%) as the most frequent symptom.
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data from symptomatic seropositive participants.

claim: Loss of smell or taste was uncommonly reported (~25% of symptomatic subjects).
source: Loss of smell or taste was uncommonly reported (~25% of symptomatic subjects) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data from symptomatic seropositive participants.

claim: Distribution of variables recorded in CSIR-cohort (prevalence of smoking, diet, physiological parameters like ABO blood group type) was similar to the national averages.
source: Apart from gender and age, distribution of the other variables recorded in CSIR-cohort (prevalence of smoking, diet, physiological parameters like ABO blood group type) was similar to the national averages and the sample can be considered representative (Patidar and Dhiman, 2021; Mohan et al., 2018; Government of India, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patidar and Dhiman, 2021; Mohan et al., 2018; Government of India, 2014.

claim: The CSIR-cohort sample can be considered representative.
source: Apart from gender and age, distribution of the other variables recorded in CSIR-cohort (prevalence of smoking, diet, physiological parameters like ABO blood group type) was similar to the national averages and the sample can be considered representative (Patidar and Dhiman, 2021; Mohan et al., 2018; Government of India, 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with national data, supported by citations.

claim: Outsourced staff performing support services were more likely to be seropositive.
source: Outsourced staff performing support services such as security, housekeeping, etc., and subjects using public transport were more likely to be seropositive.
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Subjects using public transport were more likely to be seropositive.
source: Outsourced staff performing support services such as security, housekeeping, etc., and subjects using public transport were more likely to be seropositive.
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In males, smoking was associated with lower seropositivity.
source: In males, smoking and vegetarian diet was associated with lower seropositivity.
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In males, vegetarian diet was associated with lower seropositivity.
source: In males, smoking and vegetarian diet was associated with lower seropositivity.
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Blood group type was reported for 7496 subjects.
source: Blood group type was reported for 7496 subjects.
evidence: This is a description of the available data.

claim: Blood group distribution of subjects in the study was similar to national reference based on a recent systematic review.
source: Blood group distribution of subjects in our study was similar to national reference based on a recent systematic review (Patidar and Dhiman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Patidar and Dhiman, 2021.

claim: Seropositivity was significantly different between different blood groups.
source: Seropositivity was significantly different between different groups, being highest for blood group type AB (10.19%) followed by B (9.94%), O (7.09%), and A (6.97%).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of blood group data.

claim: Seropositivity was highest for blood group type AB (10.19%).
source: Seropositivity was significantly different between different groups, being highest for blood group type AB (10.19%) followed by B (9.94%), O (7.09%), and A (6.97%).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of blood group data.

claim: Blood group O was found to be associated with a lower seropositivity rate, with an odds ratio of 0.76 (95% CI 0.64–0.91, p=0.018) vs. non-O blood group types.
source: Blood group O was found to be associated with a lower seropositivity rate, with an odds ratio (OR) of 0.76 (95% CI 0.64–0.91, p=0.018) vs. non-O blood group types
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of blood group data.

claim: Blood group B appeared to be at high risk with an odds ratio of 1.36 (95% CI 1.15–1.61, p=0.001).
source: while B appeared to be at high risk with an OR of 1.36 (95% CI 1.15–1.61, p=0∙001).
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of blood group data.

claim: Blood group A had an odds ratio of 0.78, but the association was not found to be significant (p=0.10).
source: While blood group A had an OR of 0.78, the association was not found to be significant (p=0.10)
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of blood group data.

claim: Blood group AB had an odds ratio of 1.27, but the association was not found to be significant (p=0.35).
source: and a similar observation was made with blood group AB (p=0.35), it had an OR of 1.27 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on logistic regression analysis of blood group data.

claim: Rh factor was not found to have a significant association with seropositivity (p=0.35).
source: Rh factor was not found to have a significant association with seropositivity (p=0.35).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of Rh factor data.

claim: Of 607 subjects whose samples were collected again at 3 months, anti-nucleocapsid antibody levels were similar or higher for most.
source: Of 607 subjects whose samples were collected again at 3 months, anti-nucleocapsid (anti-NC) antibody levels were similar or higher for most, with 17 (2.8%) becoming seronegative (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 3 months follow-up, 17 subjects (2.8%) became seronegative.
source: Of 607 subjects whose samples were collected again at 3 months, anti-nucleocapsid (anti-NC) antibody levels were similar or higher for most, with 17 (2.8%) becoming seronegative (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 3 months follow-up, 34 subjects (5.6%) did not have neutralizing activity based on a surrogate measure (>20% inhibition of receptor-spike protein binding).
source: In contrast, 34 subjects (5.6%) did not have neutralizing activity based on a surrogate measure (>20% inhibition of receptor-spike protein binding; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Of 175 subjects whose samples were collected again at 5–6 months, 8 (4.6%) became seronegative.
source: Of 175 subjects whose samples were collected again at 5–6 months, 8 (4.6%) became seronegative (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At 5-6 months follow-up, neutralizing activity was not present in 31 (17.7%) subjects.
source: In contrast, neutralizing activity was not present in 31 (17.7%) subjects (Figure 4D, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal follow-up measurements shown in Figure 4D.

claim: By September 2020, more than a hundred million Indians were likely to have recovered with at least partial immunity.
source: Between our study and the other national serosurvey at the same time, more than a hundred million Indians were likely to belong to this category.
evidence: This is an extrapolation based on the seropositivity rates from this study and the ICMR survey.

claim: The subsequent nationwide decline of new cases starting in October 2020 can be well understood through the existence of a large pool of recovered Indians with at least partial immunity.
source: The subsequent nationwide decline of new cases starting in October 2020 can be well understood through these observations.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the seropositivity findings to the epidemiological trajectory.

claim: The fraction of recovered subjects with resistance to reinfection was more than double among people performing high-contact jobs and using public transport.
source: As shown in our study, the fraction of such recovered subjects with resistance to reinfection was more than double among people performing high-contact jobs and using public transport.
evidence: This is an inference based on the odds ratios for occupation and transport mode.

claim: As of January 2021, despite the onset of winter and new year festivities, India has not seen major outbreaks.
source: As of January 2021, despite the onset of winter and new year festivities, India has not seen major outbreaks.
evidence: This is a statement about the epidemiological situation at the time of writing.

claim: Almost 20% of RT-PCR-proven asymptomatic infections develop transient antibody responses.
source: and expect that downward adjustments for national demographics will be counterbalanced by upward adjustments for almost 20% of RT-PCR-proven asymptomatic infections who develop transient antibody responses (Koopmans and Haagmans, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koopmans and Haagmans, 2020.

claim: No major difference was observed in seropositivity among different age groups.
source: The workforce in our cohort comprised adult population, and no major difference was observed in seropositivity among different age groups or those with comorbidities.
evidence: This is based on analysis of age-stratified seropositivity data.

claim: No major difference was observed in seropositivity among those with comorbidities.
source: The workforce in our cohort comprised adult population, and no major difference was observed in seropositivity among different age groups or those with comorbidities.
evidence: This is based on analysis of comorbidity-stratified seropositivity data.

claim: Males were found to be more susceptible to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Males were found to be more susceptible, in agreement with other published reports (Ortolan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the study's data and supported by citation to Ortolan et al., 2020.

claim: There were fewer females in the study.
source: However, there were fewer females in our study and many of the occupational responsibilities with higher chances of exposure, like that of security personnel, were skewed towards males.
evidence: This is a description of the study population demographics.

claim: Many of the occupational responsibilities with higher chances of exposure were skewed towards males.
source: However, there were fewer females in our study and many of the occupational responsibilities with higher chances of exposure, like that of security personnel, were skewed towards males.
evidence: This is a description of the occupational distribution in the study population.

claim: On iteratively ran regression models, gender was not found to be a predictor for seropositivity.
source: On iteratively ran regression models, we did not find gender to be a predictor for seropositivity.
evidence: This is based on the results of the iterative logistic regression analysis.

claim: Most studies found that the O blood group is associated with a lower risk of infection or severity.
source: Most studies found that the O group is associated with a lower risk of infection or severity and blood group A was reported to be high risk in some studies (Zhao et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Göker et al., 2020; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Zhao et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Göker et al., 2020; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).

claim: Blood group A was reported to be high risk in some studies.
source: Most studies found that the O group is associated with a lower risk of infection or severity and blood group A was reported to be high risk in some studies (Zhao et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Göker et al., 2020; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Zhao et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020; Göker et al., 2020; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).

claim: A meta-analysis observed positive association with A blood group.
source: In a meta-analysis authored by Golinelli et al., 2020, they observed positive association with A blood group, while blood group O was to be associated with lesser positivity using a random effects model.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Golinelli et al., 2020.

claim: A meta-analysis found blood group O was associated with lesser positivity using a random effects model.
source: In a meta-analysis authored by Golinelli et al., 2020, they observed positive association with A blood group, while blood group O was to be associated with lesser positivity using a random effects model.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Golinelli et al., 2020.

claim: A study from India observed blood group O to be associated with less mortality.
source: Another study from India observed blood group O to be associated with less mortality while blood group B with higher mortality when they analyzed the national data available (Padhi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Padhi et al., 2020.

claim: A study from India observed blood group B to be associated with higher mortality.
source: Another study from India observed blood group O to be associated with less mortality while blood group B with higher mortality when they analyzed the national data available (Padhi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Padhi et al., 2020.

claim: It has been proposed that a fiber-rich diet may play an important role in COVID-19 through anti-inflammatory properties by modification of gut microbiota.
source: It has been proposed that a fiber-rich diet may play an important role in COVID-19 through anti-inflammatory properties by modification of gut microbiota (Conte and Toraldo, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Conte and Toraldo, 2020.

claim: A recent review has highlighted the role of trace elements, nutraceuticals, and probiotics in COVID-19.
source: A recent review has highlighted the role of trace elements, nutraceuticals, and probiotics in COVID-19 (Jayawardena et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jayawardena et al., 2020.

claim: The negative association with smoking has been reported elsewhere, but not shown to be causal.
source: The negative association with smoking has been reported elsewhere, but not shown to be causal (Fontanet et al., 2020; Makoto Miyara et al., 2020; Rossato et al., 2020; Petrilli et al., 2020; Farsalinos et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies (Fontanet et al., 2020; Makoto Miyara et al., 2020; Rossato et al., 2020; Petrilli et al., 2020; Farsalinos et al., 2020).

claim: Seropositivity is an imperfect marker of infection risk.
source: Further exploration is necessary before reaching any conclusions, especially since seropositivity is an imperfect marker of infection risk and may equally well be explained by altered antibody response and dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of seropositivity as a measure.

claim: The stability of antibody response is poorly understood, especially in India.
source: The stability of antibody response is poorly understood, especially in India (Figueiredo-Campos et al., 2020; Seow et al., 2020; Deshpande et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Figueiredo-Campos et al., 2020; Seow et al., 2020; Deshpande et al., 2020.

claim: While anti-NC antibodies provide long-lasting evidence of viral exposure or infection, about 20% of seropositive individuals lack meaningful neutralization activity after 5–6 months.
source: Our data shows that while anti-NC antibodies provide long-lasting evidence of viral exposure or infection, about 20% of seropositive individuals lack meaningful neutralization activity after 5–6 months.
evidence: This is based on the longitudinal follow-up data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Using more stringent measures (more than 30% inhibition of surrogate receptor-spike protein binding), the loss of neutralization may be even higher.
source: Using more stringent measures (more than 30% inhibition of surrogate receptor-spike protein binding), the loss of neutralization may be even higher.
evidence: This is a speculation based on applying a different threshold to the neutralization data.

claim: The loss of neutralization activity may be related to recurrence of outbreaks in March 2021, after the peak in September 2020.
source: We speculate that this may be related to recurrence of outbreaks in March 2021, after the peak in September 2020.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation about the relationship between waning immunity and future outbreaks.

claim: India had a large pool of recovered immune subjects by September 2020, especially among its high-contact workers and people using public transport.
source: The aggregate seropositivity of 10.14% in our multicentric study suggests that India had a large pool of recovered immune subjects by September 2020, especially among its high-contact workers and people using public transport, leading to a decline in new infections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the seropositivity data and occupational/transport associations.

claim: The large pool of recovered immune subjects led to a decline in new infections.
source: The aggregate seropositivity of 10.14% in our multicentric study suggests that India had a large pool of recovered immune subjects by September 2020, especially among its high-contact workers and people using public transport, leading to a decline in new infections.
evidence: This is an inference connecting seropositivity to the decline in new infections.

claim: The duration of immunity may not be sufficient to prevent future outbreaks, even in highly affected regions.
source: However, the duration of such immunity may not be sufficient to prevent future outbreaks, even in highly affected regions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed decline in neutralization activity over time.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Human Ethics Committee of CSIR-IGIB vide approval CSIR-IGIB/IHEC/2019–20.
source: The longitudinal cohort study was approved by the Institutional Human Ethics Committee of CSIR-IGIB vide approval CSIR-IGIB/IHEC/2019–20.
evidence: This is a statement about the ethical approval of the study.

claim: The participation was voluntary.
source: The participation was voluntary, and participants had to fill an online informed consent with a consent to publish and share findings and deidentified data.
evidence: This is a description of the study design and consent process.

claim: The minimum sample size for estimating seropositivity of about 5% with 10% precision (0.005) with 95% confidence was calculated to be 7300.
source: Online statistical tool was utilized to calculate the minimum sample size for estimating seropositivity of about 5% with 10% precision (0.005) with 95% confidence to be 7300 (Dhand and Khatkar, 2014).
evidence: This is based on a sample size calculation, with citation to Dhand and Khatkar, 2014.

claim: 10,427 adult subjects working in the CSIR laboratories and their family members enrolled for the study based on voluntary participation.
source: In this study, we enrolled >10,000 subjects. 10,427 adult subjects working in the CSIR laboratories and their family members enrolled for the study based on voluntary participation.
evidence: This is a description of the study enrollment.

claim: Antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 NC antigen were measured using an Electro-chemiluminescence Immunoassay (ECLIA)-Elecsys Anti-SARS-CoV-2 kit (Roche Diagnostics).
source: Blood samples (6 ml) were collected in EDTA vials from each participant, and antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 NC antigen were measured using an Electro-chemiluminescence Immunoassay (ECLIA)-Elecsys Anti-SARS-CoV-2 kit (Roche Diagnostics) as per the manufacturer's protocol.
evidence: This is a description of the laboratory methods used.

claim: The Elecsys Anti-SARS-CoV-2 assay is considered a method of choice when a single test is to be deployed.
source: This approved assay is considered a method of choice when a single test is to be deployed (Krüttgen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Krüttgen et al., 2021.

claim: A Cut-off index COI >1 was considered seropositive.
source: A Cut-off index COI >1 was considered seropositive.
evidence: This is a description of the threshold used for defining seropositivity.

claim: Positive samples were tested for neutralizing antibody response using GENScript cPass SARS-CoV-2 Neutralization Antibody Detection Kit.
source: Positive samples were further tested for neutralizing antibody (NAB) response directed against the spike protein using GENScript cPass SARS-CoV-2 Neutralization Antibody Detection Kit (GenScript, USA), according to the manufacturer's protocol.
evidence: This is a description of the laboratory methods used.

claim: A value of 20% or above in the neutralization assay was considered to have neutralizing ability.
source: A value of 20% or above was considered to have neutralizing ability.
evidence: This is a description of the threshold used for defining neutralizing activity.

claim: Changes in test positivity rate (TPR) are a relatively robust marker of the local level of transmission when the level of testing is variable.
source: Changes in test positivity rate (TPR) are a relatively robust marker of the local level of transmission and are preferred when absolute number of tests or test rates are variable, as was the case here.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for using TPR as a metric.
